profile.feeling: Zero — the Arabic word behind English zero and cipher.

examples.tr: My phone number starts with a zero.

etymology.text: A semantic loan from Sanskrit शून्य (śūnyá, “zero”, literally “empty”) — Arabic صِفْر, “empty”, translated the Indian idea (Wiktionary).

funFacts: English zero and cipher, German Ziffer, Russian цифра and Turkish sıfır all go back to صِفْر (via Medieval Latin zephirum and cifra).
The digit zero in the Arabic digits used in the Middle East (٠١٢٣٤٥٦٧٨٩) is a dot: ٠.
pitfalls: In Eastern Arabic digits ٠ (a dot) is 0 and ٥ (a small circle) is 5 — do not read ٥ as zero.

profile.feeling: One — and with a noun, “only one, a single”.

senses.def: one (counting; after a noun it stresses “one single”: كِتَابٌ وَاحِدٌ)

funFacts: Hebrew אֶחָד (eḥad) matches the other Arabic “one”, أَحَد (in 11: أَحَدَ عَشَرَ, and “one of”: أَحَدُ الطُّلَّابِ).
Turkish tevhit (belief in one God) is Arabic تَوْحِيد, from the root و ح د of وَاحِد.
pitfalls: “A book” or “one book” is normally just كِتَابٌ; وَاحِدٌ after the noun adds “only one”.
1 and 2 agree with the noun (masculine وَاحِدٌ, feminine وَاحِدَةٌ) and come after it, like an adjective.
subtleties: The other “one”, أَحَد (feminine إِحْدَى), is used in 11 and in “one of”: إِحْدَى الطَّالِبَاتِ (one of the female students).

profile.feeling: Two — mostly hidden in the noun itself: the dual.

senses.def: two (with a noun the dual alone says “two”: كِتَابَانِ)

funFacts: Hebrew שְׁנַיִם / שְׁתַּיִם (shnáyim / shtáyim) is the same word, also dual in form.
Monday is يَوْمُ الِاثْنَيْنِ, “day two”: the Arabic week starts on Sunday.
pitfalls: “Two keys” is مِفْتَاحَانِ (the dual); *اِثْنَانِ مِفْتَاحٌ is wrong. اِثْنَانِ after the dual only adds emphasis.
It is itself a dual: اِثْنَانِ (nom.) / اِثْنَيْنِ (acc., gen.); feminine اِثْنَتَانِ / اِثْنَتَيْنِ.
The i- is a hamzat al-waṣl: after a vowel it is not pronounced (وَاثْنَانِ, wa-ṯnāni).

profile.feeling: Three — the first number with the reversed gender.
funFacts: Hebrew שָׁלוֹשׁ (shalósh) is the same Semitic word.
Tuesday is الثُّلَاثَاءُ, “the third (day)”, from the same root ث ل ث.
pitfalls: 3–10 take the opposite gender: the form with ة goes with masculine nouns (ثَلَاثَةُ كُتُبٍ), the form without ة with feminine nouns (ثَلَاثُ غُرَفٍ) — decide by the singular of the noun.

funFacts: Hebrew אַרְבַּע (arbá) is the same word.

profile.feeling: Ten — and its plural عَشَرَات, “dozens of”.

examples.tr: There are ten students in the class.

funFacts: Hebrew עֶשֶׂר / עֲשָׂרָה (éser / asará) is the same word.
عَشَرَات (tens) means “dozens of, many”: عَشَرَاتُ النَّاسِ.
pitfalls: 3–10 take the opposite gender: the form with ة goes with masculine nouns (ثَلَاثَةُ كُتُبٍ), the form without ة with feminine nouns (ثَلَاثُ غُرَفٍ) — decide by the singular of the noun.
Not only the ة changes: with masculine nouns عَشَرَةُ (ʿašaratu, three short a's), with feminine nouns عَشْرُ (ʿašru).

funFacts: Hebrew builds the teens the same way, unit + ten: שְׁלוֹשָׁה עָשָׂר / שְׁלוֹשׁ עֶשְׂרֵה.
pitfalls: 11 and 12 agree with the noun (no reversal): أَحَدَ عَشَرَ كِتَابًا, إِحْدَى عَشْرَةَ غُرْفَةً; the noun is singular and accusative.
Masculine عَشَرَ (ʿašara) but feminine عَشْرَةَ (ʿašrata) — the ten changes too.

profile.feeling: Twelve — the months of the year.
funFacts: Hebrew builds the teens the same way, unit + ten: שְׁלוֹשָׁה עָשָׂר / שְׁלוֹשׁ עֶשְׂרֵה.
pitfalls: 12 is the only teen with cases: اِثْنَا عَشَرَ (nom.), اِثْنَيْ عَشَرَ (acc., gen.); feminine اِثْنَتَا / اِثْنَتَيْ عَشْرَةَ.
It agrees with the noun, like 2: اِثْنَا عَشَرَ رَجُلًا, اِثْنَتَا عَشْرَةَ بِنْتًا.

examples.tr: There are thirteen students in the class.

etymology.text: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *ʿiśrū-; compare Hebrew עֶשְׂרִים (esrím) and Aramaic עֶסְרִין (Wiktionary).

funFacts: In Arabic and Hebrew alike, “twenty” looks like a plural of “ten”: عِشْرُونَ, עֶשְׂרִים.
pitfalls: -ūna is the nominative; the accusative and genitive end in -īna: عُمْرُهُ عِشْرُونَ سَنَةً, but بَعْدَ عِشْرِينَ دَقِيقَةً. In speech you mostly hear -īn.
The tens have no gender and take an accusative singular: عِشْرُونَ طَالِبًا, عِشْرُونَ طَالِبَةً.

profile.feeling: A hundred — the round number of percentages and prizes.

senses.def: a hundred (followed by a genitive singular: مِائَةُ كِتَابٍ)

examples.tr: There are a hundred books in the library.

etymology.text: From Proto-Semitic *miʔat-. The frequent spelling مائة has a silent alif, added to keep the word apart from مِنْهُ in the old undotted script (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Hebrew מֵאָה (meá) is the same word.
Two hundred is the dual: مِائَتَانِ.
pitfalls: Write مائة, read miʾa: the alif is silent. The spelling مِئَة (the same word) is also common.
After 100 and 1000 the noun is genitive singular: مِائَةُ طَالِبٍ, not *مِائَةُ طُلَّابٍ.
subtleties: 300–900 are written as one word: ثَلَاثُمِائَةٍ (three hundred), with the singular مِائَة.

profile.feeling: A thousand — the number of the Nights.

senses.def: a thousand (followed by a genitive singular: أَلْفُ كِتَابٍ)

examples.tr: There are twenty thousand (people) in the town.

funFacts: Hebrew אֶלֶף (élef) is the same word.
The letter أَلِف (ʾalif) is a different word: only the vowel tells أَلْف (thousand) from أَلِف (the letter).
pitfalls: Its plural آلَاف is used after 3–10: ثَلَاثَةُ آلَافٍ (3000); two thousand is the dual أَلْفَانِ.
After أَلْف the noun is genitive singular: أَلْفُ شَخْصٍ.

profile.feeling: Abundance — many, much, a lot; as كَثِيرًا, the everyday “a lot, very much”.

senses.def: many, much, a lot of (after the noun, agreeing with it: كُتُبٌ كَثِيرَةٌ, أَصْدِقَاءُ كَثِيرُونَ)
a lot, very much (the accusative كَثِيرًا as an adverb: شُكْرًا كَثِيرًا)

examples.tr: I have many friends in Egypt.

collocations.tr: many people (lit. many of the people)
often (lit. in many of the times)

phrases.meaning: the many beat the brave; numbers win

synonyms.nuance: numerous — mostly in writing: الْعَدِيدُ مِنَ الْكُتُبِ (many books)

etymology.text: From the root ك ث ر (“to be many”); Wiktionary gives no older origin. Wiktionary lists its elative أَكْثَر (more, most).

funFacts: Turkish ekseriyet (majority) and ekseriya (mostly) come from أَكْثَر, the comparative of this word.
pitfalls: People take the plural كَثِيرُونَ (أَصْدِقَاءُ كَثِيرُونَ); things take the feminine singular كَثِيرَةٌ (كُتُبٌ كَثِيرَةٌ) — the rule for non-human plurals.
As the adverb “a lot” it does not agree: شُكْرًا كَثِيرًا, never *شُكْرًا كَثِيرَةً.
subtleties: Two ways to say “many books”: كُتُبٌ كَثِيرَةٌ (adjective after the noun) and كَثِيرٌ مِنَ الْكُتُبِ (“much of the books”, with مِنْ, lesson 11) — the second is very common in writing.

profile.feeling: Not much, not many — scarcity, modesty, brevity.

senses.def: few, little (after the noun, agreeing with it: كُتُبٌ قَلِيلَةٌ, أَصْدِقَاءُ قَلِيلُونَ)

examples.tr: Water is scarce in the desert.

phrases.tr: the best speech is what is short and to the point

phrases.text: قَلِيلٌ دَائِمٌ خَيْرٌ مِنْ كَثِيرٍ مُنْقَطِعٍ
phrases.tr: a little that lasts is better than a lot that stops
phrases.meaning: steady small efforts beat big bursts

etymology.text: From the root ق ل ل (q l l); related to Aramaic קלל (Wiktionary). Its elative is أَقَلّ (less, least).

funFacts: Hebrew קַל (kal, light, easy) belongs to the cognate root ק ל ל.
pitfalls: Arabic does not split “few” and “a few” as English does: قَلِيل covers both, and the context gives the tone.
Things in the plural take the feminine singular (كُتُبٌ قَلِيلَةٌ), people the plural (قَلِيلُونَ).
subtleties: The same root gives أَقَلّ (less, the least) and قَلَّمَا (rarely).

profile.feeling: A little, a bit — modest and polite.

senses.def: a little, a bit (how much: with verbs and adjectives); “a little of X” = قَلِيلًا مِنْ X
for a little while, a moment

synonyms.nuance: somewhat, to some extent — more formal
a bit — the everyday word in many dialects (Egypt, the Levant, the Gulf), not MSA

etymology.text: The adverbial accusative of قَلِيل (“little, few”), from the root ق ل ل (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Like German ein bisschen and Greek λίγο, it answers both “how much?” and “how long?” (wait a little).
pitfalls: The final -an is part of the word: qalīlan, said qalīlā at a pause; written with tanwīn and an alif: قَلِيلًا.
For “a little of something” add مِنْ (lesson 11): قَلِيلًا مِنَ الْمَاءِ, or قَلِيلٌ مِنَ الْمَاءِ when it is the subject.
subtleties: The accusative -an turns adjectives into adverbs: كَثِيرًا (a lot), قَلِيلًا (a little), جِدًّا (very).

profile.feeling: Totality — all, the whole, every single one.

senses.def: all, the whole (with a definite noun after it: كُلُّ الطُّلَّابِ, all the students)
every, each (with an indefinite singular after it: كُلَّ يَوْمٍ, every day)

phrases.tr: may you be well every year
phrases.meaning: the greeting for holidays and birthdays

synonyms.nuance: all, the whole of a group (جَمِيعُ الطُّلَّابِ) — never “every”
all without exception — official, written style (كَافَّةُ الْمُوَاطِنِينَ)

etymology.text: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *kull-; compare Akkadian kalûm and Classical Syriac ܟܾܠ (kul) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Hebrew כָּל / כֹּל (kol, all) is the same word.
Turkish külliye (a complex of mosque and schools) is Arabic كُلِّيَّة (in Arabic today: a faculty, a college), from this word.
pitfalls: كُلّ is a noun: the noun after it is genitive (كُلُّ الْبُيُوتِ), and كُلّ itself takes the case of its place in the sentence (subject: كُلُّ).
Definite after it = “all the …” (كُلُّ الْكُتُبِ); an indefinite singular = “every” (كُلُّ كِتَابٍ).
subtleties: It can also come after the noun with a pronoun: الطُّلَّابُ كُلُّهُمْ (the students, all of them).

profile.feeling: A part, not the whole — some of them.

senses.def: some, a part of (with a definite plural or mass noun after it: بَعْضُ الطُّلَّابِ, some of the students)

examples.tr: Some of the students are here.

synonyms.nuance: several — a few countable things: عِدَّةُ كُتُبٍ

etymology.text: From the root ب ع ض; Wiktionary gives no older origin.

funFacts: Turkish bazı (some) and bazen (sometimes) come from بَعْض and بَعْضًا.
pitfalls: بَعْض is a noun: the word after it is genitive and usually definite — بَعْضُ الْكُتُبِ (some of the books), not *بَعْضُ كُتُبٌ.
Do not mix it up with بَعْدَ (after): ض and د.
subtleties: بَعْضَ الشَّيْءِ (somewhat) is the formal “a little”.
